text: At 8:30 the recruiter sends you forty résumés for an analyst role, labeled “the best of the best.” The first one’s experience: “summer camp counselor.” Get through them all by lunch?
left: Hand them off to the team

text: The candidate joins the interview from his car at a red light. “I can hear you perfectly, go ahead.” Horns are blaring behind him. Carry on?
Asked “What’s your biggest weakness?”, the candidate says honestly: “I can’t stand pointless meetings.” You have seven on your calendar today. Hire him?
The director wants the role filled within a week: “Just hire somebody, we’re short-staffed.” Good candidates: zero. There is one who’s “fine.”
A candidate’s test assignment is excellent, but the file metadata lists a completely different author. On the call he’s very convincing. What now?
The recruiter asks you to cut the interview to 20 minutes: “He’s hot on the market, he has three other offers.” Your question list runs an hour and a half.
At the end of the interview the candidate asks: “Why did the last person in this role leave?” The last person left because of your director.
Your final candidate wants an offer 40% above the salary band. She’s the best you’ve seen in six months. The director is on vacation and not answering.
The team wants to sit in on interviews. Now six people are on every call, and each one asks about their favorite framework.
A candidate you rejected a month ago sends a three-page essay on why you made a mistake. The director is cc’d.
The recruiter is thrilled: the candidate accepted! He can only start in three months, though — “wrapping up projects.” Your project is on fire now.
The candidate sends a heartfelt thank-you note after the interview. Very touching. Last line: “I need an answer by tomorrow or I’ll take another offer.”
The head of sales recommends a “great guy” — his nephew. The résumé is weak, but saying no will sour things with sales for ages.
Third day in a row of four interviews a day. The candidates have merged into one person who says “I’m a team player.” Pause hiring?
The candidate turns out to be your old classmate — the one you used to copy homework from. He recognizes you and grins broadly.
HR asks you to rewrite the job ad: “Too many requirements, nobody’s applying.” The director wrote the requirements and is very proud of them.
Your strongest employee asks you not to hire a candidate: “We worked together before. It won’t work.” The candidate is objectively good.
The job board offers a “premium listing” for half your quarterly training budget. Without it you get almost no applicants.
The candidate asks more questions than you do. About the budget, about turnover, about your management style. You start sweating.
The director texts in the evening: “Checked your finalist’s socials. Travels too much. Won’t he take vacation right away?” You’ve already given a tentative yes.
A junior candidate writes under “expectations”: “Become your manager within a year.” Says it without a hint of a smile.
The recruiter suggests an “interview marathon”: five candidates back to back, half an hour each, no breaks. “We’ll fill the role faster.”
On a video interview, someone behind the candidate is clearly whispering answers. Sometimes you can even see a hand holding a note.
The team chat is discussing a candidate: “He said in the interview our processes are a mess.” People are offended. Then again, he’s basically right.
In the final round the candidate says he can start tomorrow — but only remotely, from another time zone. His morning is your midnight.
The recruiter wants a feedback form for every candidate: 18 fields, including “culture fit, 1 to 7.” There were twelve candidates.
A candidate solved the test task better than your team solved the same problem for real six months ago. The team can see that too.
Evening. You need to call three finalists and tell two of them “no.” You could send HR’s template email. Or call in person.
The director wants to interview a candidate “together with you.” Midway he starts describing projects you haven’t even approved yet.
A candidate with an offer asks for a call to “clarify a couple of things.” The couple turns out to be seventeen, including laptop color.
A neighboring team lead proposes a swap: “My analyst for your designer — they’d fit better with us.” Neither candidate knows.
9 p.m., the recruiter writes: “Candidate changed his mind and took a counteroffer.” Week six of the search ends with nothing.
An employee wants to refer a friend and collect the referral bonus. In the interview the friend mixes up basic concepts.
A three-hour invite lands: “Interviewer Calibration.” Everyone rates how everyone else asks questions.
The candidate suddenly asks: “Could I watch your team work for a couple of hours?” The team is not at its best today.
HR reports: during a reference check, your finalist’s former manager said one word — “Well…” — and then stopped answering the phone.
The new hire’s first day. No laptop, no access, badge coming tomorrow. He’s looking at you hopefully. What now?
right: Send him to read the wiki

text: The new hire asks if there’s a “how everything works” document. There isn’t. It all lives in three people’s heads, and one of them is on vacation.
On his third day the new hire stays until 9 p.m. Says he “wants to get up to speed faster.” The team is already giving him looks.
HR wants you to throw the new hire a “welcome breakfast” at 8:30, with balloons. The new hire is an introvert — it shows even in his résumé.
left: Keep it to a quiet coffee

text: The assigned buddy complains: “The new guy asks a question every five minutes, I can’t get anything done.” The new guy complains the buddy never talks.
On day one the new hire proposes rewriting half your processes: “At my last job we did it differently.” The team tenses up and goes quiet.
The sysadmin says the new hire’s access will take two weeks: “Ticket queue.” The new hire has read the whole wiki and counted the ceiling tiles.
The new hire messages in the evening: “So I don’t need to do anything until Monday, right?” Wrong. But technically you never gave him a task.
At his first stand-up the new hire accidentally mentions a mistake a veteran has been hiding for a month. The silence is deafening.
right: Take it to a private chat

text: You promised the new hire a detailed 90-day onboarding plan. He starts in an hour. There is no plan. There is a file called “plan_final_2.”
The new hire finished his first task in a day instead of a week and wants the next one. You haven’t come up with a next one.
right: Ask him to study the code

text: Near the end of probation the new hire admits: “I don’t think I’m cutting it.” From what you’ve seen — he is, but barely.
The director wants to meet the new hire personally — right at his first stand-up, with the question “How exactly will you be useful to this company?”
right: Talk the director out of it

text: The new hire left a labeled lunch container in the kitchen. Someone ate half. He’s shocked and asks if that’s normal here.
The new hire asks if he can leave at six too, like his contract says. The whole team stays until eight, though nobody ever asked them to.
The new hire shows up in a suit and tie. The whole team wears hoodies. He sheepishly asks about a dress code. There isn’t one. There is a director, though.
The team started a separate chat “without the new guy,” so as “not to overload him.” He happened to see the chat’s name in a shared folder.
The director wants the new hire to “wow” a key client from day one. The new hire is still looking for the restroom.
In the evening the new hire sends you a twenty-page “team process analysis” concluding “a lot could be optimized.” A lot means you.
A senior employee refuses to mentor: “I don’t get paid for it, it’s just more work.” There’s nobody else who could mentor.
left: Get him a bonus for it

text: HR sends a 64-item onboarding checklist and wants the new hire’s progress ticked off daily. Item 41: “Has felt the company values.”
The new hire’s probation ends tomorrow. You never held a single feedback session. He’s waiting for a decision.
1:1 with an employee at 9:00. He’s brought a list of twelve items. You have a call with the director at 9:30. How do you fit it in?
At your 1:1 the employee says: “Everything’s fine.” Third month in a row. He won’t look up. Dig deeper?
The evening 1:1 drags on: the employee is telling you about his renovation, his cat and his complicated mother-in-law. It’s already 7:40 p.m.
Eight back-to-back 1:1s on the calendar, half an hour each. The last one ends at 1 p.m. You haven’t had breakfast.
At a 1:1 an employee asks for a raise. The salary review budget is closed until next year. She’s the best on the team.
HR rolls out a mandatory 1:1 template: six sections, a mood rating and signatures from both sides. The team is horrified.
At your 1:1 the employee says: “Can I give you some feedback?” And without waiting, pulls out a sheet of paper.
An employee cancels his 1:1 for the fourth time: “Busy now, later.” Rumor has it he’s going to job interviews.
At the morning 1:1 an employee bursts into tears over a personal situation. Stand-up is in ten minutes, and he’s presenting.
At a 1:1 you discover an employee has spent a month on a task you canceled at stand-up. He didn’t hear.
At the end of the 1:1 an employee asks: “What are my prospects a year from now?” The honest answer: “Same as now.”
The director asks what you talk about in your 1:1s and wants short minutes sent to him.
At a 1:1 an employee complains about a colleague but asks you to “keep it between us.” The problem affects the whole team.
Friday evening. You’ve rescheduled your 1:1 with a quiet employee three times. He hasn’t objected once. That’s what worries you.
An employee shows up to the 1:1 with a twenty-slide deck “On My Development.” Slide twelve shows your job title.
At a 1:1 an employee asks bluntly: “Are there going to be layoffs?” You know the answer, but promised to stay quiet until Friday.
An employee wants your 1:1s to be walks around the office. It’s November, wet snow, and you’re in thin shoes.
Video 1:1. The employee forgot his camera is on and has been playing a phone game for half an hour while you talk. You can see everything.
An employee says he “doesn’t need 1:1s at all, everything’s clear.” The other five attend dutifully.
At a 1:1 an employee asks to work noon to 9 p.m.: “I’m a night owl, mornings I’m a vegetable.” Your stand-up is at 10.
At a 1:1 an employee asks why a colleague with the same experience earns more. The numbers really are different, and you don’t know why.
The director wants you to use 1:1s to “motivate people to work overtime without extra pay.” You look at this week’s list of meetings.
The new hire texts at 7:50: “Can’t find the office. I’m at the building with columns.” The building with columns is the business center across the street.
The new hire asks if it’s normal to get messages at 11 p.m. Mostly, they’re from you.
In week two the new hire runs a chat poll: “What should we name our team?” The options are funny. The director will definitely hate them.
At a 1:1 an employee asks for a “stretch assignment.” Everything challenging right now is on fire, and there’s no room for mistakes.
End-of-day 1:1. The employee announces: “I’m burned out.” His quarterly report is due tomorrow.
The company hired a coach to sit in on your 1:1s “for calibration.” In front of him, your people are silent as fish.
An employee sends a 1:1 agenda: “1. My overtime. 2. Why me again. 3. Other.” The meeting is in fifteen minutes.
10:30 p.m., an employee writes: “Can we do a 1:1 tomorrow? It’s important.” No further explanation. A whole night of overthinking ahead.
At a 1:1 an employee praises you and says you’re the best manager he’s ever had. Then asks for vacation in the middle of the quarter.
At a 1:1 an employee suggests you switch to first names. You’ve kept a formal distance with the whole team for years. The others will notice.
The new hire asks in the evening if he can join the team-building event of the department next door: “It looks fun, and we don’t have one.”
The new hire’s mentor wants you to rate the new hire “below expectations” so he’ll “pull himself together faster.” The new hire is doing fine.
HR lost the new hire’s paperwork, and he’s been working “unofficially” for a week. He politely asks if he’ll be paid.
The director asks in the evening why the new hire isn’t delivering results yet. It’s the new hire’s ninth day.
At lunch the new hire asks why your previous employee quit. The whole table turns to look at you.
Sixth new hire this year. You tell the same jokes about the coffee machine and the Wi-Fi password. Maybe finally record a video?
At an evening 1:1 an employee shares an idea for the first time. The idea is bad. But he’s been silent at every meeting for two years.
An employee asks to move your 1:1 to 8:00 a.m., because after that she’s “in the flow.” You arrive at 9:30 and not a minute earlier.
At a 1:1 an employee silently places a printout in front of you: a competitor’s job ad paying 50% more. “Thoughts?”
At the end of his first month the new hire hands you a card: “To the Best Manager.” Nobody else has ever given you anything. Pin it on the wall?
Morning: two employees are fighting in ALL CAPS in the team chat over whose turn it is to be on call this weekend. Everyone else reacts with popcorn.
right: Call them both in to talk

text: Two employees refuse to work together on a project: “It’s him or me.” The project needs both. Deadline is in a week.
An employee sends a long evening message: a colleague took credit for her idea in a meeting with the director. The colleague is your most valuable developer.
War over the fridge: someone tossed a yogurt labeled “DO NOT TOUCH.” The team has split into two camps.
At stand-up two employees’ argument about report formats turns personal. One has already said “incompetent.” Everyone’s looking at you.
You realize half the team’s conflicts happen because you assign the same task to two people at once. Admit it?
An employee demands to be moved away from a colleague who “breathes loudly and eats nuts.” The only free desk is by the server room door.
HR tells you one of your employees filed a complaint about another of your employees. You consider both of them reasonable people.
Someone posts a meme in the group chat about “a certain colleague who’s always late.” Everyone knows who. So does he.
The team veterans have ganged up on the newcomers: no lunch invites, no answers to questions. The newcomers come to complain.
An employee feels he does all the work while a colleague gets the praise. The tracker shows he’s only half right.
An employee leaves at exactly 6:00 p.m.; the others stay until eight and resent it. Formally, there’s nothing wrong with what she does.
Two employees only talk through you: “Tell him that…” They sit two meters apart.
At the retro the team starts blaming one person for every sprint failure. He’s silent and turning red. The conversation has clearly derailed.
An employee threatens to quit if his team rival gets promoted first. The rival is the one who should be promoted — he’s stronger.
The director heard about a conflict on your team from someone else. “Why am I not hearing this from you?” You only found out yesterday.
The team is feuding over a new tool. Half want one, half want the other. You’ll have to decide, and someone will be upset.
At the department party, two employees who’ve long been at odds start loudly having it out by the karaoke. The mic is still on.
right: Act like it’s part of the show

text: An employee complains a colleague “steals” his tasks in the tracker and closes them faster. The colleague says: “I’m just helping.”
An employee refuses to attend stand-ups “as long as he’s there.” He is her ex-boyfriend and your analyst.
right: Ask her to leave it at home

text: You catch yourself avoiding the kitchen because your people are always arguing there. Lunch at your desk again?
You finally delegate the director’s report. The employee takes three times as long and does it twice as badly as you would. Redo it?
Morning realization: this week you did twenty of your team’s tasks and none of your own. Time to learn to delegate?
You gave a task to an employee, he gave it to the intern, the intern gave it to an AI. The result reached you full of mistakes.
You delegated a client presentation. At 9 p.m. the employee writes: “I’ve started it.” The pitch is tomorrow at nine.
An employee hands back a delegated task: “This isn’t part of my job.” You checked — technically, it isn’t.
In a meeting the director asks about a task you delegated. You don’t know its status. The employee is sitting next to you, silent.
The employee you delegated to sends “is this okay?” every half hour. That’s the seventh tonight.
You delegated the quarterly report but spent all morning checking every line over the employee’s shoulder. He’s visibly nervous.
An employee takes on everything he’s offered and finishes nothing on time. Today he raised his hand for a new project again.
You delegated a task and forgot. So did the employee. The tracker didn’t: 21 days overdue, and the director is looking at the board right now.
You need to delegate a dull spreadsheet reconciliation. Nobody wants it. The veterans refuse; the newbie can’t handle it.
An employee did a delegated task nothing like you imagined, but the result is even better. The director wants it “as agreed.”
You go on vacation in two days. Everything only you know how to do is written down nowhere. Start delegating right now?
An employee offers: “How about I run stand-ups instead of you?” Sounds helpful. Also sounds like the start of a coup.
You hand out the week’s tasks, and within an hour three people come to swap. The result is the same plan, just scrambled.
The director reminds you in the evening: “Delegate, but you’re accountable.” The employee you assigned the task to just went on sick leave.
You delegated the team lunch. The employee booked a restaurant where the average bill equals your weekly salary.
right: Go and don’t think about it

text: For the first time you let an employee present to the director instead of you. He nailed it. The director asks: “So why do I need you?”
10 p.m.: “Can’t decide which font to use in the report. Could you pick?” You delegated him the entire report.
Your unofficial deputy wants the role made official. He won’t take the title without a raise, and there’s no budget.
An employee does everything she’s assigned perfectly, but has never once taken initiative. The director wants “more proactivity on the team.”
8 p.m. You’re rewriting an email your report already sent to a client, “so it’s done right.” The client got it hours ago.
Two employees argue over who’ll answer the director’s questions while you’re on vacation. Each is sure you promised them.
A team conflict has escalated into a sticker war in the group chat. Hundreds of smirking cats. The director is in this chat.
An employee demands a written order for every task: “So there’s no dispute later.” He usually gets about thirty tasks a day.
An employee grabbed a task you’d delegated to a colleague and did it overnight: “He’d never have made it.” The colleague is furious.
Friday evening. Your “only I can do this” list has grown to twenty items. Half are ordering water and checking receipts.
An employee brings a problem and waits for a solution. You read that you should ask: “How would you solve it?” He looks at you with longing.
The employee you put in charge of hiring an intern hired her little sister. The sister is doing pretty well, though.
The director hands down the quarterly OKR: “Increase customer satisfaction by 300%.” Nobody knows how to measure it. Object?
Finance wants your department KPI broken down into individual KPIs per person. Your team only works together; nothing can be measured separately.
Filling in the KPI sheet in the evening, you see: honestly, the department hit 87% of target. If you “count it right,” it’s 103%.
First thing in the morning: “My KPIs are impossible to hit. Can we revisit them?” He’s right — you wrote them at night.
At the OKR session the team came up with 14 key results. The director wants three max. Everyone defends their own.
Last day of the quarter. You’re one closed deal short of KPI. The client will sign if you give a discount you can’t get approved.
The new KPI dashboard on the big office screen shows your department in red. The cause is a formula error, but every director walks past it.
As taught at training, you set an ambitious OKR and hit 70%. The director sees 70% and asks why not 100%.
An employee hit 150% of her KPIs, but the rest of the team is dragging the number down. She asks if she’ll get a separate bonus.
HR announces that from this quarter, every manager’s KPIs include a “team happiness index,” measured by a monthly survey.
The director wants “number of initiatives” added to team KPIs. A week later you have 40 initiatives, including “Move the water cooler.”
Evening, quarterly KPI deadline. You notice one metric was calculated with the old formula all quarter. With the new one: minus 20%.
An employee has started “optimizing KPIs”: closing one-line tasks in the tracker to boost the count. Pretty numbers, zero value.
A neighboring team lead proposes a deal: he’ll put your task in his KPIs, you put his in yours. “Easier reporting for both of us.”
For the first time this year, you reread the OKRs set in January. Half are irrelevant, and one is about a product shut down in March.
The director wants the department KPIs daily at 9:00 instead of monthly. Compiling them by hand takes an hour every morning.
The team asks to keep KPIs at last year’s level: “We’re already maxed out.” The director wants 25% growth.
At 9:30 p.m. the director sends a screenshot of a competitor’s KPIs: “Why theirs and why ours?” The competitor’s numbers come from an ad brochure.
Finance wants the quarterly plan by Friday. The director says the strategy won’t exist until next month. Plan for what?
Morning stand-up on the quarterly plan. The team proposes a realistic plan. Yesterday the director promised upstairs twice as much.
The quarterly plan is ready: 47 slides, three scenarios, a Gantt chart. In the morning the director will ask for “one page.” Cut it now?
Finance sent back your quarterly plan marked “too optimistic.” The director sent back the same plan marked “not ambitious enough.”
An employee pitches a “seriously cool” project for the quarterly plan, but it has nothing to do with company goals. He’s on fire about it.
A strategy offsite on the quarterly plan at a country hotel. The first four hours are a leadership team-bonding quest.
Evening message from the director: “Add one more project to the quarterly plan. No resources, but you’ll manage.” The team is at 120% capacity.
The shared quarterly plan spreadsheet. Overnight someone moved every deadline a month forward. The edit history says: “Anonymous.”
At the quarterly plan review, another department claims half your tasks are their responsibility. The director wants a decision.
At the end of the day an employee quietly asks: “Can we really get everything in the plan done?” You know you can’t. So does she.
Quarterly retro. Turns out 40% of the plan got done, but lots of unplanned work did too. How do you show the director?
The director asks for a “contingency reserve” in the quarterly plan. Then crosses it out: “We won’t have any contingencies.”
The night before the quarterly plan review, you realize the grand total is off by an order of magnitude. An extra zero, or a missing one?
The team runs a betting pool on what percent of the plan the department will hit. Bets range from 30% to 70%. Nobody went higher.
At 8 p.m. the director forwards the quarterly plan with one edit: “Deadlines two weeks earlier.” No explanation, no resources.
You discover your key result “launch the service” depends on another department that doesn’t have it in its OKRs. At all.
Friday night an employee writes: “I’ve figured out how to hit the quarterly plan. We just need to work the weekend.” He wants the whole team.
Morning. The quarterly plan is approved, signed and sent out. An hour later the director announces a “shift in priorities.” The plan is obsolete by lunch.
The finance guy wants the “expected economic impact” of every task in the plan. Including “Update the slide template.”
Final hours of the quarter. To hit the “tickets handled” KPI, you could split each ticket into three. The team suggests doing exactly that.
An employee proposes dropping “response speed” from the department KPIs — quality matters more. The director adores speed.
The team’s quarterly bonus depends on KPIs you agreed to in a hurry. The team is falling just short. Call the director and plead?
The director asks you to prepare an “explanation for missing the plan” in advance. The quarter just started.
At the quarterly retro an employee says: “Our problem is the goals change every two weeks.” Everyone nods. The director changes the goals.
The analyst brings a forecast: at the current pace, the quarterly plan will be complete on March 14 next year. Today is October 1.
In the evening the team asks to stop filling in daily OKR progress reports: “They eat an hour a day.”
The director wants to roll out “OKRs for every employee, including the cleaners.” Your department gets to be the “pilot.”
You wake at 5:40 a.m. realizing you forgot to put three employees’ vacations in the quarterly plan. You submitted it yesterday.
Finance proposes tying team bonuses to revenue your team has roughly zero influence on. “But at least it’s the same for everyone.”
An employee sends a proposal to revise the OKRs, with detailed math. The math is right, but it means admitting the goal was a mistake.
The director at the morning meeting: “I don’t like the word ‘plan.’ Let’s call it a ‘roadmap.’” Every document is titled “Plan.”
You hit 100% of your quarterly plan. Instead of praise the director says: “So the plan was too easy.” Next one: 150%.
Morning news from finance: the department budget is cut by 15%. “You decide where to save.” Options: training, bonuses, or the holiday party.
Near year-end, the department has unspent budget left. If it’s not spent by December 31, next year’s budget will be smaller.
Reviewing department expenses in the evening, you find a six-month subscription to a service nobody uses. You signed up for it.
An employee wants the company to pay for a conference in another city: “Everyone will be there.” It costs as much as the whole team’s quarterly training budget.
Finance rejected the request for new monitors: “Justify the economic impact.” The old monitors flicker, and two employees have sore eyes.
7:30 p.m. email from finance: “Urgently send next year’s budget forecast by 9:00 a.m.” The template is a 14-tab spreadsheet.
The director wants the budget padded by 30% “just in case.” Finance wants it cut by 10%. You’re the one defending it.
Procurement demands three vendor quotes for a $5 stapler. No quotes, no payment.
The team asks for a holiday dinner budget. Finance allocated enough for pizza and soda — if you pick it up yourself.
The department is 3% over budget. Finance demands a written explanation. The overspend came from a decision the director made and forgot.
Finance introduces a rule: any expense over $100 needs three signatures. Your employee urgently needs to travel and can’t buy a ticket.
You’re redoing the budget spreadsheet for the twelfth time because finance keeps changing the format. Now they want thousands instead of dollars.
Accounting demands original receipts from a business trip six months ago. The employee who went quit three months ago.
The director wants department savings that “won’t upset anyone.” The only line you can really cut is the team’s quarterly bonuses.
The finance guy calls at 8 p.m.: “If you don’t use your contractor budget within a week, another department gets it.” You only need a contractor in spring.
The contractor writes at 8:15 a.m.: “Running a bit behind, we’ll deliver in a month.” The deadline was yesterday, and the project was already shown to the director as done.
The contractor delivered. Everything looks great, but an hour later you discover half of it was copied from free templates.
Friday night the contractor sends an invoice twice the contract amount: “The scope grew.” It grew because of your change requests.
A vendor’s account manager invites you to a “business breakfast” at a fancy restaurant. You happen to be choosing a supplier for the year. Go?
Contractor tender: one company is half the price, the other more reliable. Finance wants the cheap one. The team wants the reliable one.
The contractor wants access to all your systems “for a couple of hours.” Security takes a week to review such requests.
The contractor made a group chat with your team and posts there at 6 a.m. Your people ask if they have to reply before work.
The contractor shows up with a new account manager. Everything you agreed over six months will have to be explained all over again.
A vendor promises 20% off if you sign by midnight. Legal has gone home, the director isn’t answering.
The contractor delivered and sent a 30-question satisfaction survey. No survey, no sign-off; no sign-off, no payment.
Mid-project, the contractor secretly offers your best employee a job. The employee told you himself.
An employee offers to replace the contractor: “I’ll build it over the weekend.” The contractor wants $50,000; the employee wants pizza.
A vendor writes that prices go up 40% starting tomorrow, “in line with market conditions.” The annual budget is already approved.
At the demo the contractor shows an interface you’ve never seen. “This is what you asked for.” You definitely did not ask for this.
In the evening the contractor asks you to sign off on completed work “for old times’ sake,” though part of it isn’t done. The director never checks sign-offs.
Procurement found a vendor 3% cheaper than the current one. Switching takes three months and means reconfiguring everything you built over two years.
At a meeting the vendor rep gives you a branded hoodie, a travel mug and an umbrella. Compliance requires declaring gifts worth over $40.
The freelancer you work with vanished for a week. Today he resurfaces: “I was in the mountains, no signal.” The project is on fire.
The director picked a contractor for your project himself: “My old classmate, great guys.” The guys’ portfolio is empty.
The contractor offers to “optimize” the contract: drop the late-delivery penalties in exchange for 5% off. Finance loves the discount.
The vendor’s service went down at 8 p.m.; their support works until 6. Your team is sitting there staring at their screens.
The contractor wants the weekly status call moved to 7:30 a.m.: their office is in another time zone. At 7:30 you’re usually still in pajamas.
Finance hasn’t paid the contractor for two months: “It’s in the queue.” The contractor threatens to stop work, and blames you.
In the evening you notice the contractor billed 15 hours of calls. You remember three. Each was ten minutes long.
Next year’s budget needs new headcount. Finance says: “Only if you cut someone you already have.”
The director wants to buy an expensive system he saw at a friend’s company. It solves problems you simply don’t have.
The contractor invites your team to their company party “as a sign of friendship.” Compliance advises caution.
Finance proposes freezing all department spending until the end of the quarter. Your work software subscription expires next week.
An employee paid for a year of hosting with his own card “because otherwise everything would’ve crashed.” Accounting won’t reimburse without a contract.
You realize your annual budget is last year’s spreadsheet plus 10%. Like everyone’s. Like last year.
The contractor brings an intern to the morning meeting who’ll “just listen.” The intern asks the most questions and records everything on a voice recorder.
The finance guy wants you to explain at the board meeting why your department spent more on coffee than marketing spent on ads.
In the evening a vendor sends an 80-page draft contract titled “Standard terms, nothing special.” It has to be signed in the morning.
The director wants you to present the budget in German “because it sounds more serious.” The entire board speaks only English.
right: Gently talk him out of it

text: The contractor admits they lost the source files for the entire project during an office move. No backup. They probably have one, but won’t say.
This morning Sales promised a client a feature that doesn’t exist and won’t this year. The client is already thanking your team in a reply-all.
Marketing is launching an ad campaign for your team’s product — and is only now finding out it exists. “Why weren’t we invited?” they yell.
In the managers’ chat, the head of the next department writes: “Your team blew the deadline again.” It was his team that blew it.
For a month, accounting and your team have been emailing about who should process the invoices. 23 people are cc’d, including the CEO.
Meeting with IT. Both sides came with decks on why the other side is to blame. Yours is 15 slides, theirs is 40.
The head of sales invites you to a bar “just to talk.” You know tomorrow the board decides whose department gets an extra headcount.
The warehouse won’t ship your client’s order without a paper request with a blue stamp. The director has the blue stamp; the director is on a plane.
Legal has been reviewing a contract for two months; your team can’t start the project without it. Version five came back with a comma fixed.
Late at night Marketing posts about your team’s “revolutionary product.” So far the product exists only as mockups.
IT updated a system without warning and broke everything for your team. IT says: “We sent a newsletter.” Nobody reads the newsletter.
A neighboring team lead quietly poached your best employee. The employee is happy; you’re left with a vacancy and a grudge.
Evening email: the head of an adjacent department “informed” the director about your team’s problems. You weren’t cc’d.
Sales asks your team for an urgent “small customization” for a client. Small means two weeks of work, and it’s not in your plan.
You and HR have spent three months arguing over who owns onboarding. Meanwhile the newcomers are onboarding however they can — which is not at all.
You catch yourself writing an email to the next department for the third time, angrier each time. It’s 9:10 p.m. Send it?
right: Delete it and go to bed

text: Support forwards every hard customer question to your team. 74 tickets this week. Nobody on your team signed up to do support.
Finance and Sales are fighting over numbers, and the director asks you, “the neutral party,” to judge. You’re not neutral: your bonus depends on both.
The head of marketing proposes an alliance one evening: “You back my project at the board, I back yours.” His project is frankly weak.
At the leadership meeting you’re asked to shorten deadlines because “the other team is already ready.” They’re ready on paper — you’ve seen their code.
Security blocked your team’s cloud storage. No explanation. Files are due to the client in two hours.
The director asks you to “make up” with the head of the next department. You never fought; you just haven’t said hello in three years.
The director wants a status report every morning. Every morning he asks about what was in the report, because he doesn’t read it.
Monthly report to the director. Nothing to brag about this month, but there are three reasonable failures. How do you frame them?
9 p.m., you’re finishing the report upstairs. One section left: “Key Team Achievements.” You’ve been staring at it for twenty minutes.
The CEO unexpectedly asks you to report on your department in person. Your director finds out and asks to be “invited too.”
The director wants only good news in the monthly report. There’s one bad item, but it’s big: a key client is leaving.
The director sent your report back with one note: “Add more energy.” Nothing else. It’s already evening.
The director forwards your report to the CEO under his own name. You find out from the CEO’s thank-you email to him.
The CEO wants to switch from text reports to a dashboard. Your team spent a month building it. The CEO looks at it and asks for text.
Evening message from the director: “Good report, but where are the risks?” Last time you wrote about risks, he said: “Don’t be so dramatic.”
You realize the report for upstairs and the report for the team tell completely different stories about the same month.
The director wants the report “yesterday.” The data won’t be ready until tomorrow. You can eyeball an estimate or wait for facts.
The director sends a 9-minute voice message with edits to the report. It begins with “Quickly.” You’re on the subway and your earbuds are dead.
At the morning meeting the CEO praises your team for a project. The director sits beside him nodding as if it were his project.
The director wants you to rate every employee weekly on a five-point scale and send it to him. The employees don’t know.
You sent the quarterly report and suddenly spot last quarter’s revenue figure in it. The director has already replied: “Excellent!”
The director opens the morning with: “I hear your team does nothing.” He won’t say who said it.
You’re invited to the board to present your department’s work in three minutes. Your material is built for twenty.
Friday, 6:30 p.m. The director wants an “analytical memo” on the department by Monday. You can ruin your own weekend or the team’s.
Sales complains to the director that your team is “dragging its feet.” The same day you find an email showing they withheld data for a month.
Without warning, the call center routed its hotline to your team for the duration of their team-building. The phone has been ringing since 8 a.m.
At 7 p.m. Logistics reports that the shipment for your project is delayed. They knew this morning, “but didn’t want to upset you.”
HR demands your team’s signatures in paper safety-briefing logs. The logs are on another floor; the team is remote.
Marketing stole the name your team came up with for a project and used it for their promo. Now the project has to be renamed.
right: Come up with a new one

text: The team asks you to talk to the department next door, which blasts music across the floor after six. It’s their “creative evening.”
The director wants a new section in the weekly report: “What I personally did for the company.” You won a tender, but he did the paperwork.
Finance and Legal email you at the same time, each demanding the contract be approved by them first. Both set a noon deadline.
The director wants the report as “one page, but with all the details.” You shrink the font to 8 and squeeze the margins.
Sales invites you to a joint stand-up to “improve communication.” They spend ninety minutes showing off their wins, then ask how you’re doing.
In the morning you realize last week’s report was never sent. The director didn’t notice. Send it now, or act like that was the plan?
First thing in the morning the director demands the whole team come in on Saturday “to show loyalty.” There’s no work on Saturday, just loyalty.
right: Pass it on to the team

text: At the all-hands, the CEO publicly criticizes your employee’s mistake. The employee is sitting in the audience, going pale.
At 10 p.m. the director messages your employee directly, bypassing you, with a task “for tomorrow morning.” The employee asks you what to do.
In the morning you learn the director wants to “shake up” your team. Your two best people are on the transfer list. Tell them now?
The director wants cameras on your team “for workload statistics.” The team is already nervously joking about a reality show.
The team learned that the project they spent three months on is being shut down from above. Everyone’s upset. You don’t know why yet.
The director demands employees reply within five minutes during work hours. Your analyst is in the middle of building a complex model.
The CEO suddenly wants to “sit with the team” and watch you work. That day the team is mid-argument about the product’s future.
In the evening the director proposes “making an example” of an employee who missed a deadline. It was missed because of the director’s own decision.
Someone accidentally forwards a director’s email to the team chat: “the team can’t cut it.” Everyone read it in ten seconds. Deleted, but too late.
The director wants your team to take another project, “since you’re so fast.” You’re fast because you work until midnight.
You realize you’ve spent the whole year as a buffer between the director and the team. The buffer is wrung dry. Let one punch through, for once?
The director wants to personally run your team’s stand-up on Monday, “to energize them.” The last one like that ended with two resignations.
At the director’s request, HR asks you to rank your employees “from best to worst.” They won’t say why. Everyone knows why.
The director wants you to personally make sure nobody on the team leaves before 7 p.m. Your contract ends at 6, like everyone’s.
In the morning an employee tells you the director yelled at her in the elevator over an email you told her to send.
The director wants to hear from your team “without you” at an open-door session. He writes everything down in a notebook.
In the evening the team asks why the quarterly bonus was canceled. The decision came from above; you were just told after the fact.
The director wants your team to file hourly written reports: what you did 9 to 10, 10 to 11, and so on.
There’s a layoff rumor going around. Employees corner you at the coffee machine. You know exactly as much as they do.
In the evening the director says: “You need to cut one person from your team. Pick by morning.” The team doesn’t know yet.
Today’s the layoff announcement. You rewrote your speech three times and still don’t know how to start. The meeting is in ten minutes.
HR is holding a layoff conversation with your employee and asks you to be there “for support.” The employee is an old friend.
A laid-off employee asks for a recommendation letter in the evening. Honestly, his work was mediocre.
After the layoff announcement, the team chat is dead silent. Not a single message since morning. Nobody’s even talking about lunch.
A laid-off employee offers, as a parting gift, to tell the director exactly what she thinks of his decisions. In front of you. Right now.
The director wants the layoffs announced so “it sounds like good news for the company.” Three out of seven are being cut.
After the layoffs, the remaining four got the work of seven. In the morning they come with a question: “Is this forever?”
At the all-hands the CEO announces an “optimization.” Five minutes later you have 12 messages asking “does this affect us?”
You learn the layoffs will reach you too — in six months. The director asks you to stay quiet for now and “get the team through the project.”
In the morning an employee asks point-blank: “Am I on the layoff list?” You saw the list yesterday. He isn’t on it, but his friend is.
HR asks you to host a “farewell tea” for the laid-off employees. They themselves don’t want any tea.
A laid-off employee’s last day. In the evening he hands in his badge and laptop. He’s waiting to see if you’ll say something.
Before the layoffs are announced, the director wants you to make the people on the list look bad in reports, “so it’s all justified.”
The courier who delivers documents to HR tells your team he saw “some kind of lists.” Panic is rising.
In the evening the team goes to a bar to “pay respects” to the laid-off colleagues, who also came. You were invited, but hesitantly.
The morning after the layoff announcement. You have to run a normal stand-up as if nothing happened. Or as if something did?
After the layoffs, the director wants to “boost team spirit” and allocates a pizza budget. It covers one pizza for four people.
An employee who survived the layoffs confesses in the evening: “I feel guilty that they kept me.” He’s almost in tears.
The CEO announces in the morning: “There will be no more layoffs.” He said exactly the same thing a week before the last ones.
The director won’t let your people go to a conference because “they’ll find new jobs there right away.”
The director messages you in the evening: “Why did your employee like a competitor’s post?” The employee liked a photo of a cat.
The director wants your team in by 8:00 on Mondays for “morning meetings with leadership.” Voluntary. Mandatory.
The CEO wants to move your employee into his own department “as a promotion.” A step up for him, a hole for you.
Friday evening. Defending your team is good, but the director has called you “the defense attorney” three times this month. Not as a compliment.
You arrive in the morning to find the team has picked over the departed colleagues’ desks for souvenirs. New hires arrive in a week.
HR sends a layoff announcement script. In it you’re supposed to say: “This was a difficult decision by leadership.” Nobody asked you.
right: Say it in your own words

text: A laid-off employee hands you a notebook as he leaves: “Everything I know about the system. You’ll need it.” It’s 120 handwritten pages.
A week after the layoffs, you catch yourself assigning tasks to people who no longer work here. The tracker doesn’t stop you.
The director wants you to give the laid-off people a “reason” so it looks fair. The real reason: a bad quarter for everyone.
HR announces only one person from your team can be promoted this cycle. There are three candidates, and all three know about the cycle.
An employee has been waiting two years for a promotion. You’ve promised “next cycle” three times. He politely asks which cycle that will be.
In the evening the director asks who on the team you see as your successor. The honest answer: nobody. That looks bad for you both.
An employee turns down a promotion: “I don’t want to manage people, I want to do the work.” The director finds that odd.
The promotion committee wants your candidate justified in one paragraph. You wrote three pages. The committee never reads past a paragraph.
In the evening an employee learns his colleague got promoted instead of him. He writes: “Can we talk tomorrow morning.” With a period at the end.
You promoted an employee to senior specialist. Now her former peers don’t invite her to lunch. She asks how to make things like before.
The director wants to promote one of your people whom he personally likes. You like him less — he presents brilliantly but does little.
You realize you’ve never told the team how promotions actually work here. Because you don’t fully know yourself.
A freshly promoted employee starts the morning bossing his former peers around, “I’m in charge now” style. Two complaints already.
HR says your employee’s promotion is approved, but without a raise: “Not the right time.” You get to tell her.
Evening message: “If I’m not promoted, I’m leaving. I already have an offer.” He’s good, but you don’t like ultimatums.
In the morning the director asks you to promote his protégée from another department to lead a stream on your team. Over your people.
An employee is up for promotion, but her strengths are invisible to the director: she quietly cleans up problems. How do you show it?
right: Write it up in a doc

text: In the evening chat the team jokes about a colleague’s promotion: “Now he’ll only drink from the boss mug.” The promoted one isn’t laughing.
Your best employee is ready for promotion. The only role above him is yours, and there’s nowhere for you to go. What now?
At the promotion committee, the head of another department says your candidate is “too young.” The candidate is 34.
An employee you didn’t promote sends a 40-item spreadsheet in the evening: “What I did this year.” Item 1: “Came to work.”
left: Go through it item by item

text: In the morning an employee thanks you for her promotion with a cake for the whole team. It’s huge, and half the team is on a diet this week.
HR wants your employee’s new title rewritten because “Senior Lead Principal Specialist” doesn’t fit in the system.
left: Come up with a shorter one

text: In the evening the director wants to discuss promoting “one of yours,” but it turns out he means your rival from another department.
An employee got promoted and immediately asks for a private office. Nobody in the building has one — not even you.
Two employees are competing for one team lead slot. Each came to you separately and asked you “not to tell the other.”
You wonder if you promoted someone just because he complained the loudest. The quiet, strong ones stayed put.
Back from parental leave, an employee learns a colleague was promoted while she was away. She asks if she has a shot.
The director wants the promotion to go to whoever is “most passionate about the work.” By his observation, that’s whoever leaves last.
A newly promoted employee calls in the evening: “I can’t handle it, put me back.” It took you six months to push that promotion through.
right: Return him to his old role

text: Four-hour “Promotion Calibration” with other managers on the calendar. Everyone will defend their own and sink everyone else’s.
An employee got promoted, but the official announcement is a month away. He’s already told everyone in the kitchen.
You’re writing the department-wide congratulations for a promoted employee. This is version six. Version one had too many feelings.
In the morning the director asks: “Why is nobody on your team growing?” He himself rejected your last three promotion requests.
An employee is excelling at a level above hers, but promoting her is “too early”: she’s been here under a year. She asks for at least a new title.
In the evening a newly promoted employee asks how to give feedback to a former friend who now reports to him. You can’t do that yourself.
HR requires three peer reviews in every promotion packet. The candidate’s peers are the same people who want his spot.
An employee offers: “Promote me with no raise, I just want the line on my résumé.” Sounds suspiciously honest.
Friday evening. A former report you once promoted is now your boss. He sends you a task for the weekend.
At the all-hands the CEO announces that all promotions this year will be “based on hackathon results.” Your team doesn’t code.
In the morning an employee asks why his colleague made senior when they started the same day. “He’s better” sounds harsh.
A newly promoted employee throws a party and invites the whole team — except the colleague who was also up for it.
In the morning the director decides to “freeze” all promotions until year-end. You already told two people they’d be promoted in December.
The team wants a transparent growth matrix: “what it takes to grow.” The director says don’t — “people will start making demands.”
Friday evening, and you realize your strongest employee should have been promoted long ago — but then the department loses its best doer.
An employee is late for stand-up for the third time this week. A new excuse each time: traffic, the cat, “the elevator left without me.” Everyone looks at you.
Friday evening the director sends an idea “to mull over until Monday”: merging your team with the one next door. You’ll be mulling all weekend.
Right off the bat the candidate asks about remote work, vacation, health insurance and lunches. Not a word about the job yet. He’s a very strong engineer.
The contractor wants a “tour” of your office for their new employees. Your team is working and doesn’t like tours.
In the managers’ chat a colleague suggests “secretly” discussing the new director. As everyone knows, no chat is secret.
Monday morning. You open your inbox: 214 emails, 180 of them cc’s “for your information.” Read them or not?
An employee proposes the key result “increase team engagement.” You ask how to measure it. He replies: “By feel.”
In the evening an employee admits she’s scared to present at the quarterly plan review. It’s tomorrow. She needs it to grow.
On his first morning the new hire asks the CEO for the Wi-Fi password in the elevator. The CEO called you.
Finance sends a report: your department leads the company in stationery spending. Turns out 90% is sticky notes used at retros.
Evening. You’ve canceled your own meeting with your mentor for the fifth time to meet with your team. The mentor asks if you’re even alive.
The team greets you in the morning with a printed letter asking to switch to a four-day week. All six signed.
The director asks for “a couple of slides” on the department for the CEO. You send two. He asks for “about fifteen more, but the same two.”
The contractor calls at 9:15 p.m. with an “urgent question”: can they change the button color in the mockup you approved a month ago?
A candidate you rejected thanks you for the detailed feedback and promises to reapply in a year. The director really liked her too.
Rumor has it your team is getting a new manager and you’re being moved “to a project.” You hear this from the cleaner.
In the evening an employee says he’s going on paternity leave in a month. You’re genuinely happy for him. But he’s running the quarter’s key project.
In the morning the director asks why your team has no “feedback culture.” Yesterday you gave him feedback and he got offended.
Your team booked the meeting room for a retro, but the department next door is in there, pretending not to see the booking. They’re on an “important call.”
right: Hold the retro in the kitchen

text: You’re at a family dinner, but your head is busy figuring out how to tell an employee his project is canceled. Your relatives ask if you’re okay.
The new hire came in at 7 a.m. to impress you. You arrive at 9:30 and find him asleep on the meeting room couch.
right: Snap a photo for the chat

text: The director approved the quarterly plan, then told the board it’s “the department’s plan,” not his. The department never planned half of it.
Friday, 6:05 p.m. Half the team is still at their computers “so as not to look worse than the others.” Nobody’s working; they’re waiting to see who leaves first.
HR asks you this morning to prepare an employee’s “success story” for the company magazine. The employee is firmly against publicity.
A neighboring team lead wants to “borrow” your analyst for two days. Last time, “two days” lasted three months.
At 8:40 p.m. the director emails with the subject “Let’s discuss your effectiveness.” The body is just a calendar link.
You open the tracker in the morning: 47 tasks in the column “Awaiting manager review.” The manager is you.
For the test assignment, a candidate sent a video with a song about your company. The song, admittedly, is catchy.
An email from another branch: “Your department is a role model — tell us how you work.” The presentation is needed by morning.
Morning. You catch yourself answering an employee with the director’s phrase you hate: “This is not up for discussion.”
At a meeting the director holds up your team as an example — and immediately announces he’ll take half its tasks “as a best practice.”
In the evening an employee writes that she got into a master’s program. Classes are Thursdays from 3 p.m. Thursday is your release day.
The contractor was forty minutes late for the morning meeting and suggests doing it in “fast mode.” There are two hours of questions.
You propose a new stand-up format: “standing, 10 minutes.” A week later everyone brings chairs and sits for half an hour.
Evening. You reread your self-review. It says: “A manager who is always available.” That’s true, and that’s the problem.
Morning. News lands in the team chat: an industry review calls your product “promising.” Everyone’s thrilled.
The laptop budget covers four. You need six. Two people will be stuck with old ones that overheated even before the pandemic.
At 7 p.m. Friday an employee delivers a task that was due Tuesday. The work is excellent. But Tuesday is gone.
The CEO sends every manager a leadership book: “Let’s discuss next week.” It’s 600 pages.
On a video call with the director, your employee forgot to mute and said: “This again.” Everyone heard. The director went silent.
In the evening the team asks if there’ll be a holiday gift. Last year it was a calendar with photos of the director.
At the morning stand-up the new hire reads out a detailed report he prepared overnight. The task was ten minutes long.
The director suggests you also take over the team next door “temporarily, until we find a manager.” The search has been going for a year.
You dream that you’re holding a 1:1 with yourself and rating yourself “below expectations.” It’s too early to get up.
An employee proposes “quiet hours” for the team until lunch: no meetings, no chats. The director loves calling before lunch.
Legal requires every employee to sign a twelve-page nondisclosure agreement. Employees demand an explanation.
A former report writes in the evening that he’s job hunting and asks for a reference. He left in a scandal, but his work was good.
The CEO catches you at the coffee machine: “So what does your department actually do?” You have until the cappuccino finishes pouring.
An employee took a day off “for personal matters.” In the evening you see his photo from a competitor’s conference online. With a speaker badge.
Last evening before vacation. You wrote the team a 12-page “in case something happens” guide. Send it, or trust them?
A candidate came to the interview an hour early and has already befriended the whole team in the kitchen. The team says “hire her now.”
Evening. You’re holding two finalists’ résumés. One has experience, the other has fire in her eyes. You must decide by morning.
The recruiter wants you to record a “Why join our team” video for the careers site. The script is written, and it includes a dance.
At the end of his first week the new hire sends you a long thank-you email plus 30 questions “to think about over the weekend.”
Morning 1:1. The employee suddenly says: “Could you tell me when I do something well? Just sometimes.”
Two employees keep arguing in the group chat even though you asked them to continue tomorrow. It’s 10:40 p.m.
You delegated contractor communication to an employee. In the morning the contractor calls you: “Your employee is rude to us. Can we deal with you?”
Evening, KPI sheet open. One employee hit 200% of his target — thanks to tasks he quietly took from his colleagues.
Morning, quarterly planning. An employee suggests, for the first time ever, asking customers what they need before planning.
At 7:45 p.m. finance asks you to “urgently explain” a large “miscellaneous” line in the budget. “Miscellaneous” is where you put everything that didn’t fit.
A vendor announces end-of-support for the product your team’s entire workflow depends on. Six months from now.
In the evening a neighboring team lead admits he deliberately stalled a shared task so his team would look better than yours. He apologizes.
At 8 a.m. the director wants the monthly report to include the team’s “emotional temperature.” Nobody knows how to measure it.
In the evening the director forwards a client complaint about your employee with one word: “Handle it.” From the email, the client is clearly in the wrong.
In the morning you announce the promotion went to the person who least expected it. He’s embarrassed. The others are trying to smile.
The evening after the layoff announcement. A laid-off employee writes: “Thanks for telling me in person, not by email.” The rest ask about themselves.
In the morning the CEO gathers the managers: “Who’s ready to take a pilot project from scratch?” Everyone stares at the table. Except you.
In the evening an employee confesses she’s been working two jobs for two months because of her mortgage. She’s coping, but very tired.
In the morning the new hire asks if he should also put an inspirational quote in his email signature, like the director. The director loves quotes.
For the first time in a month, you leave at 6 p.m. In the elevator you realize you have no idea what to do with an evening. Go back and finish the report?
The director asks you to “just have a chat” with the employee who wrote in an anonymous survey that the director “doesn’t listen.” The survey was anonymous.
During a demo the contractor accidentally shows their internal chat: “client is nitpicking again.” The client is you.
A year ago you promised yourself you’d be a manager who doesn’t keep the team late. It’s 8:15 p.m. and you’re setting up a call.
At a team lunch everyone is discussing salaries at once. Someone has just realized they earn less than the person next to them.
Today’s calendar: an interview, an onboarding, a budget defense, a conflict mediation and a farewell for someone leaving. Nobody scheduled lunch.
The director wants you to tell the team there will be no salary indexation this year, “but in a positive key.” You search for a positive key.
A candidate you rejected a year ago writes in the evening: “Is the role still open? I’ve grown.” As it happens, it is.
HR wants to introduce 360-degree reviews for managers. You’ll be reviewed first. Your team is giving you mysterious looks.
An employee sent a report straight to the director, bypassing you. In the evening the director thanks you for an excellent report you never saw.
Monday morning. Your to-do list says “Think about department strategy.” It’s been rolling from Monday to Monday for six months.
An employee accidentally sends you a message meant for a colleague: “Three hours of meetings with him again today, hold me back.” “Him” is you.
Late in the evening the director writes: “Your team did great. But don’t relax.” Pass the first part to the team without the second?
In the morning the contractor asks for a five-star review “in exchange for a discount on the next project.” Their work was three stars.
You’re sitting in an empty office thinking nobody appreciates you — not above, not below. Your phone shows 37 unread messages.
An employee brings you coffee every morning. Today he brought coffee and a request for a promotion. It’s your favorite coffee, too.
In the evening the team is chipping in for your birthday present. You accidentally see the chat and the amount. It’s huge.
Finance demands an employee return a bonus paid “by mistake.” He already spent it, and it was finance’s mistake.
The evening before the quarterly plan defense. The team offers to rehearse with you. It’s 7:30 p.m. and everyone’s tired.
In the morning the director asks why your employee leaves at 5 p.m. The employee comes in at 7 a.m. The director is asleep at that hour.
Friday evening. You’re rereading the layoff email you’ll send on Monday. It’s going to be a long weekend.
The new hire’s desk still has a photo of his predecessor with a note: “Good luck, you’ll need it.” The new hire has questions.
An evening voice message: “I figured out why our process doesn’t work. Can I tell you tomorrow?” The voice message is 14 minutes long.
Morning managers’ meeting. A colleague from the next department proposes a swap: your hiring quota for his training budget.
The contractor sends the final version in the evening. File name: “final_really_final_v12_client_edits.” Open it?
Morning. You realize you can’t remember the last time you praised the team publicly. Come to think of it, the director hasn’t praised you in a while either.
At 7:50 p.m. the director wants to discuss a “strategically important matter.” It turns out to be the color of your team’s company hoodies.
In the morning an employee asks you to be her mentor in the company program. It’s another weekly meeting, but she really wants it.
Evening. Today you hired, fired, promoted, promised and refused. All in one day. Tomorrow is Friday. How do you survive?
Mid technical interview, the candidate says: “I don’t know, but I could find out in five minutes.” The other candidates confidently made things up.
At an afternoon 1:1 an employee asks you to stop praising him in front of everyone: “They tease me about it afterward.” Praise him privately?
At a meeting the contractor hands you a USB stick “with all the materials.” Security forbids plugging in outside USB drives.
right: Plug it in when no one’s looking

text: You let the team choose the offsite location. They picked glamping in the woods with no signal. The director wants to stay reachable.
Finance suggests “reallocating” your training budget to the director’s entertainment expenses. The decision is, of course, yours.
At lunch someone from another department asks if it’s true your team is “closing soon.” This is the first you’ve heard of it.
The CEO wants a proposal to reorganize your own department within a day. “No emotions, just numbers.”
Evening. For the third day in a row, an employee is the last one in the office and won’t leave even when there’s no work. Has something happened?
In the evening the team wants to celebrate getting through a brutal quarter. The director already celebrated: he sent new targets for the next one.
At 9 p.m. an email from HR: “Approve the promotion list by midnight.” It includes one of your people whom you never nominated.
right: Find out how he got there
